key_insight: Instead of compressing feedback from imperfect demonstrations into a single score, this paper uses natural-language critiques to explain what went wrong and how to improve. This richer supervision helps imitation learning learn more from suboptimal examples by capturing reasoning that scalar signals miss.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the limitation of standard imitation learning from suboptimal demonstrations, where supervision is reduced to scalar signals like confidence, discriminator scores, or weights. These signals cannot express task progress, failure causes, or corrective guidance in a human-interpretable way.
method: Replace scalar supervision with language-based critiques that describe failure modes and suggest corrections.
Use suboptimal demonstrations as input and pair them with structured natural-language feedback to guide policy learning.
Leverage the critique signal to provide richer, more interpretable supervision than conventional imitation-learning rewards or weights.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more expressive and interpretable way to learn from imperfect data, which can improve training when expert demonstrations are scarce or noisy. It also opens the door to combining language understanding with control and policy learning in a more human-aligned way.
visual_elements: Side-by-side comparison of scalar feedback vs. language critique supervision

paper_title: Language-Critique Imitation Learning from Suboptimal Demonstrations
paper_authors: Chih-Han Yang, Dai-Jie Wu, Yun-Ping Huang, Ping-Chun Hsieh, Kenneth Marino
